newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan oil spill cleanup relies on elbow grease.
newsitem.headline: Japan oil spill cleanup relies on elbow grease.

text.p: Locals living on the Sea of Japan coast have been scooping oil up in buckets and ladles in what appears to be a vain effort to try to clean up once pristine shores now fouled up by one of Japan's worst oil spills.

Experts said on Thursday that while Japan's expertise in such cleanup efforts was on a par with the West, manual labour was virtually the only means left of trying to clean up an oil slick once it has washed ashore and beguns to stain beaches.
"It's C-grade fuel oil that's been washed to shore, and its hardening because of the cold," a Maritime Safety Agency official said.
"It may not seem like much, but the most effective step we can take to retrieve oil which has reached the shore is to use manpower and scoop it up," he said.
The Nakhodka, a Russian-registered tanker, split in two and started leaking oil on January 2, but strong winds hampered efforts to try to stop the oil from spreading.
Experts said the high winds had made it impossible to fence in the spill with oil fences and that waves as high as 10 metres (yards) meant the fences would not have stopped the oil from spreading.

"The flow of the oil changes (drastically) with the wind, and the oil could have flowed to any beach within a stretch of 150-200 km (95-125 miles). Japan doesn't have enough oil fences to cover all that area," an oil industry official said.
On Thursday, new slicks came ashore across more than 300 km (190 miles) of coastline, a major fishing area and tourist spot on the Sea of Japan.

Authorities still do not know the full extent of the leakage, or the potential damage it could cause. They initially estimated that 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil leaked from the tanker. They now believe that figure may be too low.
The 13,157-tonne Nakhodka was carrying a total of 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil.
A Nippon Salvage Co Ltd official said the owner of the tanker -- Russia's Prisco Traffic Ltd -- had initially asked them to take steps to see that the broken tanker's bow would not drift to shore.
The company planned to tie the tanker to one of its ships, until a tugboat dispatched by Prisco could take the broken vessel back to Russia.
Strong winds scuttled the plan, he said.
The stern is believed to have sunk about 115 km (70 miles) offshore, while the bow has been grounded off the shore at the fishing port of Mikuni, Fukui prefecture.
Nippon Salvage is a private company jointly owned by major Japanese insurance and shipping companies.
Foreign experts appear to agree that Japanese authorities are doing all they can.
Hugh Parker, London representative of the International Tanker Owners' Pollution Federation Ltd, who arrived in Japan to survey the scene, said the cleanup work was going very well.
"It is more advanced than I thought it would be," he said.
Japan's worst oil spill was in 1971, when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil were spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata on the Japan Sea.
